text: A cinder cone grows when fragments thrown from a vent fall back around it. Many have a bowl-shaped summit crater.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A composite volcano builds up through successive layers of lava and fragmented erupted material, producing a steep-sided mountain.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Fluid lava can spread across broad distances before cooling, gradually constructing a volcano with a low, shieldlike profile.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Viscous lava can pile up near its vent rather than flow far, forming a dome.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: After erosion removes much of a volcano, hardened material that filled its conduit can remain as a projecting volcanic neck.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Magma can fill cracks on a volcano's flanks and solidify as dikes. These ribs of rock can remain after softer surrounding material erodes.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/types.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: At a divergent plate boundary, plates move apart. New crust can form as molten material rises into the opening.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Volcanoes and Plate-Tectonics Theory; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/tectonics.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: At a subduction boundary, one plate descends beneath another. Many chains of volcanoes lie above these converging margins.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Volcanoes and Plate-Tectonics Theory; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/tectonics.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A moving plate can carry older volcanoes away from a volcanic hot spot while new ones form above it, leaving an island chain.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Volcanoes and Plate-Tectonics Theory; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/tectonics.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: At a strike-slip boundary, plates move horizontally past one another.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Volcanoes and Plate-Tectonics Theory; https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/volc/tectonics.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Groundwater can dissolve limestone, gypsum, or salt, enlarging cracks into cavities. Landscapes shaped by this process are called karst.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, What is a sinkhole?; https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-a-sinkhole. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A sinkhole is a depression without a natural surface outlet; water entering it typically drains underground.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, What is a sinkhole?; https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-a-sinkhole. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A cavity can grow underground while the surface still appears intact. Collapse occurs when the remaining roof can no longer support the land above.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, What is a sinkhole?; https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-a-sinkhole. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Karst drainage may run through enlarged fractures and caves. A disrupted surface stream network can reflect a connected drainage system below ground.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey Circular 1139, Hydrologic Cycle and Interactions; https://pubs.usgs.gov/circ/circ1139/htdocs/natural_processes_of_ground.htm. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A moraine is a ridge of debris deposited along a glacier's margins. Ridges left after retreat can mark former ice limits.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey Professional Paper 387-B, Recent activity of glaciers of Mount Rainier; https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/pp387B. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: When two glaciers merge, debris bands from their adjoining edges can join into a medial moraine down the combined glacier.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Glossary of Glacier Terminology; https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2004/1216/text.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A tarn is a lake occupying a cirque basin, commonly left after the glacier that carved the hollow has melted.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Glossary of Glacier Terminology; https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2004/1216/text.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A rock glacier is a glacierlike mass of rock debris, often filling a valley beneath a cirque.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: US Geological Survey, Glossary of Glacier Terminology; https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2004/1216/text.html. Consulted 2026-10-13.
